convs.s: The ability to get customers separates the businesses that live from the ones that don't — and it cannot be outsourced.

convs.b: Bet on yourself; protect the ship.
convs.s: Take extreme but survivable risk. Ruin is the only unforgivable loss, and staying in the game is most of winning.
There are no great ideas — only bad ones, and built ones. Tell everyone, iterate fast, and let the feedback do its work.
Build with people smarter than you, share a future with them rather than a past, and get good at asking for help.
Nobody buys a product; they buy a story about themselves. The telling is half the work.
A boring niche you are genuinely curious about beats a glamorous one you will quit. Interest is the only fuel that lasts that long.

book.t: Our issue is rarely figuring out what to do. It is figuring out why we don't do the things we already know we should.
Beyond all the resources, you need a big burning why to carry you through — otherwise the what and the how become the excuse.
A good life has a simple test: are you excited to get up?
Labour without a vision is just exhaustion.
In the beginning it isn't about perfection. It's about speed and momentum.
Almost nobody regrets starting a business. The regret belongs to the people who kept meaning to.
If there is no risk, there is no story.
There is no such thing as a great business idea — there are bad ideas, and there is execution.
Tell everybody your idea. The feedback is worth more than the secrecy, and the social contract holds you to the work.
The best businesses take something already succeeding and figure out how to do it differently and better.
Don't pitch your solution — go into their problems first. They cannot know the solution yet.
The single biggest thing separating successful businesses from the rest is the ability to get customers.
You can't outsource sales and marketing. The best product isn't the most used — the best-sold product is.
The golden rule of a sale: the prospect must feel you understand what they need. Everything else is decoration.
Learn how to sell. It is not an if; it is a when.
You don't sell a product, you sell a feeling. Sell the sizzle, not the steak.
Good marketing attracts and repels. If nobody is saying the opposite of you, your message isn't landing.
“I don't sell fights — I sell holy-shit moments.” Ask what you are really selling.
Investors invest in people, not ideas: people, product, progress, passion, persistence.
Don't raise money from anyone who can't afford to lose it.
Venture money is like heroin: you can end up optimising the company for raising instead of building.
Scared money does not make money.
Decide early which machine you are building: a lifestyle business that funds a life, or a liquidity business that ends in a sale. They run on different fuel.
Three hiring criteria: best at what they do, no assholes, works harder than everyone else.
The strength of a founder is building with people smarter than you — and being good at asking for help.
Share a future with people, not just a past.
It's who, not how.
book.a: Dan Sullivan's line, via Tommy Mello

book.t: Revenue is for vanity, profit is for sanity.
The hustler has to die for the leader to be born.
Early metrics can't be results. Measure activity.
It takes roughly the same years to build something massive as something small. Choose accordingly.
Protect the downside and stay in the game; most of success is still being at the table.
For a young company there is one rule that outranks the others: survive.
Find the boring thing other people find boring, be genuinely interested in it, and stay for decades.
Iterate. Don't try to be right the first time, and don't spend long on what isn't working.
It is hard to compete against someone who is just there to have fun.
Tough decisions, easy life. Easy decisions, tough life.
book.a: Jerzy Gregorek's line, via Josh Stech

book.t: Not everyone is meant to be an entrepreneur; some are meant to be intrapreneurs. Both build.

chandlery.s: Sourcing, selecting, winning, investing, building — in that order, and mostly sourcing. Hundreds looked at a year; three or four chosen.
The only differentiated things a young investor has are judgment, speed, and the willingness to be genuinely useful.
Celebrate the ones you passed on that won. It is the only honest scorecard in the business.
Write the check as if it is the last one you will ever write. If that thought changes the decision, it wasn't conviction.

chandlery.b: One diligence question survives every deal.
chandlery.s: Why is this team uniquely positioned to tackle this market?

note: A note on the trade book: it is a commonplace book, not a syllabus. These are lines written down while listening to operators — on podcasts, in classrooms, across coffee tables — kept because each one changed what I did next. “After” a name means my compressed note of their idea, not their exact words; where a line is famous in its own right, the earlier author is named. Appearing here is a debt acknowledged, not an endorsement claimed — in either direction.
